posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
I like Lyn's work but it's wrong to say bank deposit creation is "IOU" creation and not money creation. That treats state money as the only real money. It's an excessively government-centric view of how money gets created, a mistake MMT ironically makes too. Reserves sit above deposits in the settlement hierarchy, but that doesn't make deposits any less money.

It's fine to say deposits are an IOU, but deposits are absolutely money. They're the money households and businesses actually hold and spend, and they're accepted virtually everywhere. Banks make loans, which create deposits, and find the reserves after the fact. Reserve balances don't constrain lending for well-capitalized banks.

And it's not the bank's IOUs that "fail at scale." A loan creates two IOUs: the borrower's loan, which is the bank's asset, and the deposit, which is the bank's liability. It's the assets that fail, not the deposits. Asset losses are a capital problem and the Fed can't print capital. Deposit runs are a liquidity problem, and the Fed lends reserves against collateral. SVB had discount window access and still failed because unrealized securities losses had already wiped out most of its capital on a market value basis. Capital, not reserves, is the constraint for banks. Banks don't lever reserves. They lever their capital.

This matters for understanding the plumbing of the money system because deposits get created two main ways: when banks lend or buy securities, and when the Fed buys assets from nonbanks. Both are money creation, with different economic impacts. Treating bank lending as IOU stacking on top of state money diminishes how banks are major money creators in their own right and why the Fed interacts with them the way it does.

quoted.text:
Banks don't lend reserves. They lever reserves and make IOUs on top of them, rather than "creating money."

But then whenever those IOUs start to fail at scale, the central bank creates more reserves for them.

Over the past 50 years, if the US central bank held reserves flat and banks kept making money, there'd be a 160-to-1 ratio between deposits and reserves, which would be untenable. However, whenever it comes even slightly untenable, the central bank creates more reserves and swaps them for assets from banks, boosting the ratio and giving banks more lending/leveraging ability to keep it growing.

The US bank deposit-to-reserve ratio is under 4-to-1 because the central bank accommodates bank lending by creating new reserves.
